title: Sikhs in science
hook: Sikh scientists and doctors have served worldwide, like Narinder Singh Kapany in fiber optics

segments.voice: Yesterday, Milkha Singh, and your line was from orphan to athlete. Did your legs carry you somewhere briskly? Today, something even faster than a sprinter: light. Day one thousand twenty.

Somewhere under the street outside, or under the ocean, a pulse of light is racing along a strand of glass thinner than a hair. It bends around corners. It follows the cable down hills and across seabeds. Your last video call, the photo you sent this morning, the message that just buzzed in your pocket: there's a fair chance some of it traveled as light inside glass. Long before anyone streamed anything, a young Sikh physicist was asking a simple question. Can light be made to go around a bend? Today: Sikhs in science.
screen: `LIGHT RACING THROUGH GLASS.` → `AROUND CORNERS, UNDER OCEANS.` → `CAN LIGHT GO AROUND A BEND?`

segments.voice: First, the question. Light, as school science teaches, travels in straight lines. Narinder Singh Kapany, a physicist from Punjab, worked with others on bundles of very thin glass fibers that could carry light, and even an image, along a curved path. He wrote about the work under a plain name: fiber optics. Second, how it works. Inside a clear glass fiber, light hits the wall at a shallow angle and bounces back in, again and again, so it stays trapped inside and follows the fiber wherever it bends. Physicists call it total internal reflection. The light doesn't go around the corner so much as ricochet around it. Third, the wider picture. Kapany is one Sikh name in science; other Sikhs have worked as scientists, engineers and doctors, far from Punjab and in it. He also gave his time and money to Sikh art and Sikh studies, and wore the turban. Science and the Sikh story sat in the same life without a fight. Fourth, the root. At Ang 1349 of the Guru Granth Sahib, in a hymn of Bhagat Kabir, the whole world wells up from one light. Gurbani talks often about jot, the divine light in every being. A physicist studies how light moves through glass. A Sikh hears of one light moving through every life. Those are different kinds of claim, and nobody needs to blend them. But both start by paying attention to light. That's today's line: light in glass.
screen: `CAN LIGHT GO AROUND A BEND?` · `IT BOUNCES BACK IN, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · `SCIENTISTS, DOCTORS, ENGINEERS.` · `THE WORLD WELLS UP FROM ONE LIGHT.` · then, large: `LIGHT IN GLASS.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with light. Sit facing a window, a lamp, or a screen turned to its dimmest setting. Look at the light for a breath, then let your eyes close. Notice the glow that stays behind your eyelids. Breathe in, and remember that light needs something to move through: air, water, glass, the lens of your own eye. Breathe out, and let your attention rest on the faint brightness that's still there. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, and hold the thought of one light in every being. The bell holds the time.
Fiber optics. The work of Narinder Singh Kapany and others, carrying light, and even an image, through bent glass fibers. Today's word.
Your line: light in glass. Today, learn one fact about light you didn't know before, and tell it to someone over a meal. Day one thousand twenty.

howItsDone: Sikhs work in science, engineering and medicine around the world; gurbani speaks of jot, the one light in every being, which Sikhs understand as a spiritual teaching rather than a scientific one.

notes: Kapany is described as a physicist from Punjab who worked on carrying light and images through bent glass fiber bundles and wrote on it as 'fiber optics'. No dates, firsts or titles such as 'father of fiber optics' are used. Please confirm.
The claim that he wore the turban rests on his public photographs and Sikh Foundation biography; please confirm or cut.

Editor pass: cut 'one name among many Sikhs', 'as everyone learns in school', 'many gurdwaras and families honor learning' and 'kept the turban through his working life' as unsourced sweeping or duration claims; softened to what the sources support.
The hook's 'fair chance' that messages traveled as light inside glass is a soft general statement about fiber networks; check it is acceptable under the claims rule or cut.

Audit pass (2026-10-01): the fork implied Kapany alone thought of guiding light through a bend; light guided in water jets and glass was shown before him, and his early fiber work was done with colleagues (Hopkins at Imperial College).
